Chapter 3: Embracing Change and Facing Resistance
As the 19th century came to a close, the world outside China was changing faster than anyone could imagine. Railways, telegraphs, and steamships were shrinking distances, making the world seem smaller and more connected. In the bustling cities of Europe and America, brand-new ideas about government, science, and society were taking hold. For people in China, all this change was a mix of excitement... and real fear.
Inside the walls of the Forbidden City, you could feel that tension—the old ways rubbing up against the new. Some officials insisted that China’s true strength came from its ancient traditions. Others argued that if China wanted to survive, it simply had to embrace change. At the very center of this tug-of-war was Cixi, trying to balance the need for progress with the deep desire for stability.
Step by step, she started pushing for reforms to pull China into the modern age. Cixi backed the building of railways, supported new industries, and encouraged the creation of modern schools. She championed the study of science and technology, convinced that knowledge was the real key to a strong nation.
But every leap forward was met with pushback. Many in the imperial court saw these changes as a direct threat to their way of life—and their power. They warned that letting in foreign ideas might shake the very foundations of Chinese society. Cixi understood their fears, but she also realized that the world was going to change, whether China liked it or not.
Introducing the telegraph turned out to be one of the most heated battles. Some officials called it pointless, even dangerous. But Cixi saw its promise: a way to connect the massive empire and make communication faster than ever. She pushed forward, even as critics whispered and complained.
Then there was the military. China’s old armies, stuck with outdated tactics and weapons, just couldn’t keep up with foreign powers. Cixi threw her support behind new military units, trained using Western methods. But she had to tread carefully—move too quickly, and the traditionalists might revolt.
Education became a cornerstone of her efforts. Cixi firmly believed that China’s future rested on a new generation—young people who could move between Chinese and Western worlds with ease. She helped set up schools teaching foreign languages, science, and math, right alongside the classics. She even encouraged students to study abroad, hoping they’d come back with fresh ideas and practical skills.
At the heart of it, these reforms weren’t just about new machines or lessons—they were about changing how people saw themselves and their country. Cixi knew that real progress meant shifting mindsets, not just updating technology.
Still, the journey was anything but easy. Every reform sparked debate—and sometimes even open defiance. Cixi learned to compromise, often taking two steps forward and one step back. She recognized that pushing too hard could spark rebellion, but moving too slowly might leave China exposed and weak.
The palace became a constant hub of negotiation. Cixi juggled the interests of powerful families, regional leaders, and foreign diplomats—all while trying to keep everyone together. She became a master at finding just enough common ground, giving a little here and there, but never losing control.
Through it all, Cixi kept her focus: strengthening China and protecting its independence. She saw the world shifting beneath her feet, and she knew that those who refused to adapt would be left behind. Her willingness to embrace change, even with all the resistance, set her apart from so many others.
Most people outside the palace never saw the daily struggle behind these sweeping reforms. They just saw the new railways, the schools, the budding industries. But behind every change, there was a battle—fought not only with words, but with patience, persistence, and a deep understanding of human nature.
